intro: Artur Schnabel plays the Prestissimo, the E-minor middle movement of the Piano Sonata No. 30, Op. 109. Running quavers give way to exchanges between the hands, and then the opening music returns.

sections.label: A · E minor, then B minor
sections.mNote: A running melody above a strongly marked bass

sections.label: Dev · Bass line as melody
sections.mNote: Repeated B and C beneath slow-moving lines

sections.label: A′ · Opening theme returns, E minor
sections.mNote: Soft pedal released; the opening returns fortissimo.

sections.label: Coda · Staccato E-minor chords
sections.mNote: A quiet phrase builds to the closing staccato chords.

cues.title: Opening, left hand ben marcato
cues.text: The movement is in E minor, Prestissimo, and begins fortissimo after the quiet end of the first movement. Beneath the running tune the left hand is marked ben marcato (strongly marked). The second theme, in B minor, keeps the restless character of the first.
cues.evidence: Beethoven, Werke, Serie 16 No. 153, Breitkopf & Härtel, printed p. 101. The relation between the themes is discussed at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Sonata_No._30_(Beethoven).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Middle section, from the bass
cues.text: The middle section is built from the opening bass line. Repeated Bs, then Cs, sound beneath slow-moving notes above. The running quavers stop, and the hands alternate softly with the soft pedal down.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 102: repeated bass notes and una corda. Gerald Larner identifies the opening bass as the source of the middle section: https://geraldlarner.com/work/beethoven-sonata-in-e-major-op-109.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening, E minor
cues.text: The opening returns fortissimo in E minor. After passages marked una corda and sempre più piano, Beethoven writes tutte le corde, so the pianist releases the soft pedal and the hammers strike all their strings again. The first bass octaves are restored at full strength.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 102–103: una corda and sempre più piano precede the return, marked tutte le corde and ff. Score: https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/Opus109.pdf.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Maximiliane Brentano, 1821
cues.text: In December 1821 Beethoven sent the sonata to Maximiliane Brentano in Frankfurt, daughter of his friends Franz and Antonie Brentano. “A dedication!” he wrote. “But not one of those that so many people use and abuse.”
cues.evidence: Beethoven to Maximiliane Brentano, Vienna, 6 December 1821 (autograph, private ownership), printed at https://www.lvbeethoven.org/Opus109/. Her parents: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Sonata_No._30_(Beethoven).

transitions.title: Into the development of the opening bass
transitions.from: A · E minor, then B minor
transitions.how: After the B-minor second theme, Beethoven develops the opening bass. The piano holds a repeated B, the dominant of E minor, while the right hand moves into longer notes. The bass then rises to C. The Prestissimo marking remains in force, and the running quavers in both hands gradually drop away.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 102; Gerald Larner’s Op. 109 programme note identifies the opening bass as the middle section’s source. https://geraldlarner.com/work/beethoven-sonata-in-e-major-op-109

transitions.title: Soft pedal, then fortissimo
transitions.to: A′ · Opening theme returns, E minor
transitions.how: The repeated bass stops. With the soft pedal down, the hands exchange phrases marked sempre più piano and pause under a fermata. A few soft chords follow. At tutte le corde and fortissimo the opening E-minor tune returns above its bass octaves.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 102–103: una corda, sempre più piano, fermata, then the ff return. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/Opus109.pdf

transitions.title: Closing bars of the Prestissimo
transitions.from: A′ · Opening theme returns, E minor
transitions.how: In a quiet closing phrase the hands move apart. The bass steps down while the right hand plays rising chords. A crescendo leads to three short chords in E minor, marked forte staccato.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 104, final system of the Prestissimo. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/Opus109.pdf

fields.note: The edition Schnabel played from is not identified in the recording sources.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The Internet Archive description gives “recorded 22.III.1932” for the Op. 109 sonata and the Naxos Historical review gives 22 March 1932 for the same session; the Commons date field says only 1932.

fields.note: Given for the whole sonata in the review of the Naxos Historical reissue.

fields.note: The catalogue span identifies the original complete-sonata issue (the sonata runs about twenty minutes). Which sides carry this movement is not established, and the span is not shown to be the physical source of the Internet Archive MP3.

fields.note: No matrix, take or side information is established for this movement.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The transfer engineer of the Internet Archive MP3 is not identified. Mark Obert-Thorn is credited for the separate Naxos reissue, not for this transfer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is documented; the Internet Archive item was added in March 2020 and the Commons file in January 2021, which are upload dates.

fields.value: Internet Archive original: 256 kbps MP3, track 095 of Beethoven Piano Sonatas vol. 8; Commons holds an Ogg Vorbis conversion and supplies an MP3 derivative.

The programme’s pre-1963 European rule applies because the 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension. This is territorial, not a worldwide licence; US sound-recording status is not established. The exact first-publication date is not independently documented.

composer.epithet: Composer known for a symphony built from a four-note motif and for the string quartets of his last years.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, where he learned operas as a member of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was expected to return. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him ceased to exist.
